This issue is currently awaiting triage.

If a SIG or subproject determines this is a relevant issue, they will accept it by applying the `triage/accepted` label and provide further guidance.

The `triage/accepted` label can be added by org members by writing `/triage accepted` in a comment.

This looks useful, but it looks like to me that it doesn’t have reasons that are big enough to be prioritized for now. I would just keep it opened and see how many people would react and/or whether we would get more reasons apart from debuggability.

The reason I am saying this is that we have a long history but AFAIR we haven’t got a big num of this kind of requests. A few people wanted a similar stuff, and started to use kube-scheduler-simulator. I am not meaning to underrate how important this is, and actually my view is that the demand for this kind of enhanced debuggability would get bigger and bigger as WAS gets evolved mor, because WAS is complicated and users would much more likely get confused about the scheduling results. However I would say let’s wait for a right timing to start such work.

Thank you for the feedback. That makes sense.

I understand that the current motivation may not be strong enough to prioritize this work immediately, especially if the main benefit is only improved debuggability.

I will keep this issue open and try to collect more concrete use cases and signals from users.

In particular, I will try to clarify whether there are stronger reasons beyond human troubleshooting, such as:

- autoscaler and remediation tooling needing stable failure categories
- platform dashboards avoiding brittle parsing of `FailedScheduling` messages
- multi-tenant platforms exposing self-service scheduling diagnostics to application teams
- CI/CD or admission workflows detecting unschedulable workloads earlier
- observability/AIOps integrations correlating scheduling failures across clusters

I also understand the point about kube-scheduler-simulator. I will look into whether this need is better addressed by external tooling first, or whether there is still a case for a small, stable, machine-readable signal in Kubernetes itself.

Thanks again. I will wait for more reactions and additional input from SIG Scheduling before trying to move this toward a KEP.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/992d4dfeadef1c51d779d83051e1f9cb90fb9bbc/pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go#L1302-L1309

Generally, this is not a full list of the message, it has a length limitation. For large cluster, the message can be quite long sometime. Is it better to have a structured log than the pod API change?

> [kubernetes/pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/992d4dfeadef1c51d779d83051e1f9cb90fb9bbc/pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go#L1302-L1309)
> 
> Lines 1302 to 1309 in [992d4df](/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/992d4dfeadef1c51d779d83051e1f9cb90fb9bbc)
> 
>  func truncateMessage(message string) string { 
>  	max := validation.NoteLengthLimit 
>  	if len(message) <= max { 
>  		return message 
>  	} 
>  	suffix := " ..." 
>  	return message[:max-len(suffix)] + suffix 
>  } 
> Generally, this is not a full list of the message, it has a length limitation. For large cluster, the message can be quite long sometime. Is it better to have a structured log than the pod API change?

Thanks for pointing this out. That makes sense.

I agree that the current `FailedScheduling` message is not necessarily a complete source of information, especially in large clusters, because it can be truncated by `NoteLengthLimit`.

Structured scheduler logs may be a better first step than changing the Pod API, especially for detailed or high-cardinality diagnostics.

My original thought was that Pod-facing diagnostics would be useful for stable, low-cardinality signals that users and automation can consume without access to scheduler logs. But I agree that the full detailed failure information probably should not be exposed directly through the Pod API.

Maybe the problem space can be split into two layers:

- detailed diagnostics: structured scheduler logs or internal scheduler observability
- user/API-facing diagnostics: small, stable, low-cardinality summary reasons, if there is enough demand

I will look more into whether structured logging could address the main use cases before proposing any Pod API change.
